subject: Deborah
note: Evidence for Deborah's Bible figure page. Every quotation is in deborah.quotes.json and passes verify-quotes.mjs. Fetched texts are in design/saints-hub/sources/people/deborah/ (gitignored); the Fathers are the shared NPNF files. The Bible is the Berean Standard Bible (public domain); the verses quoted are copied, joined by chapter, into bsb-deborah-chapters.txt. Deborah is named in the Bible only in Judges 4 and 5 (checked against the whole BSB); Genesis 35:8 and Tobit 1:8 name other women called Deborah.

life.text: After Ehud died Israel did evil; the LORD sold them to Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor; his commander Sisera lived in Harosheth-hagoyim; Jabin had 900 iron chariots and harshly oppressed Israel 20 years.

Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel; she sat under the Palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites went up to her for judgment.
She summoned Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali: 10,000 men of Naphtali and Zebulun to Mount Tabor; God would draw Sisera to the Kishon.
Barak would go only if she went; she agreed, but the honour would go to a woman; she went with him to Kedesh; 10,000 followed him.
Sisera brought his 900 chariots to the Kishon; Deborah told Barak 'this is the day'; Barak came down Tabor with 10,000; the LORD routed Sisera; Sisera fled on foot; not a man of the army was left.

Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite (at peace with Jabin), gave Sisera milk, covered him, and drove a tent peg through his temple as he slept; she showed Barak the body; God subdued Jabin; Israel's hand grew stronger until they destroyed him.
life.source: Judges 4:17-24 (BSB). The Catholic Encyclopedia (1908) says the prophecy of 4:9 refers to Jael, not Deborah.

life.text: The song of Judges 5, sung by Deborah and Barak 'on that day': the LORD from Seir, rain from the heavens (5:4), 'a mother in Israel' (5:7), the roll of tribes that came (Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar, Naphtali) and stayed (Reuben, Gilead, Dan, Asher), Meroz cursed, the stars fighting and the Kishon sweeping them away, Jael blessed, Sisera's mother at the window, the closing prayer, 40 years of rest.
life.source: Judges 5 (BSB). Britannica calls the song 'perhaps the oldest section of the Bible' and a glimpse of Israel in the 12th century BC; the Catholic Encyclopedia calls it 'this very early poem'.

life.text: Josephus: Deborah means a bee, Barak lightning; a storm of rain and hail blew in the Canaanites' faces; 'thus was this victory gained by a woman, as Deborah had foretold'; Barak and Deborah died about the same time.
life.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 5, chapter 5 and chapter 6.1 (Whiston). josephus-antiquities-5.txt.

life.text: Pseudo-Philo's Biblical Antiquities gives Deborah a farewell speech; she is buried in the city of her fathers; the people mourn her 70 days with the lament 'Behold, a mother is perished out of Israel'. M. R. James (1917) dates the book after AD 70.
life.source: Pseudo-Philo, Biblical Antiquities 33 (tr. M. R. James, 1917); James's introduction, section 6, Date. pseudo-philo-biblical-antiquities-30-33.txt, pseudo-philo-james-intro-date.txt.

numbers.text: iron chariots of Jabin, under Sisera
men of Naphtali and Zebulun who followed Barak down Tabor
years of rest after the song, following 20 years under Jabin; then Midian

tidbits.text: Deborah = bee (Strong's 1683, from 1682), Barak = lightning (Strong's 1301; Josephus), Lappidoth = torches (Strong's 3941).

The Catholic Encyclopedia: Deborah 'was thus a judge in the ordinary sense of the word'; the other judges bear the title as 'deliverers and leaders', 'no mention being made of ordinary judicial functions'.
Talmud, Megillah 14a: seven prophetesses, Sarah, Miriam, Deborah, Hannah, Abigail, Huldah and Esther.
tidbits.source: Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 14a (the Gemara: 'Who were the seven prophetesses? ... Sarah, Miriam, Deborah, Hannah, Abigail, Huldah, and Esther'), read at Sefaria (people/abigail/sefaria-megillah-14a.txt). The Jewish Encyclopedia 'Deborah' text on disk does not hold the list.

tidbits.text: Rabbinic reading of the palm: being a woman she would not judge in private but in the open air where all could assemble (Tanna debe Eliyahu).
Jael is 'Most blessed among women' (Judges 5:24); Elizabeth to Mary, 'Blessed are you among women' (Luke 1:42).
Other Deborahs: Rebekah's nurse (Genesis 35:8, BSB); Tobit's grandmother (Tobit 1:8, WEB, a book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles). Used as a fact.
A later rabbinic story (Tanna debe Eliyahu) makes Lappidoth, the 'torches' man who made wicks for Shiloh, Barak himself. Used in the circle.

said.text: 'Deborah, a woman, waged war', in a list of judges who acted 'In the might of this Spirit'.
'Women have preserved whole nations; for Deborah and Judith exhibited successes worthy of men'.

'It is not sex, but valour which makes strong.' Ambrose calls her a widow and Barak her son (sections 44-46); Judges gives her husband Lappidoth and Barak's father Abinoam. De Viduis is dated 377 in the NPNF chronology.

said.who: Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts 5 (read, not used)
said.text: At Pentecost the gift of prophecy passes to women 'not as of old ... limited to just one or two individuals, as Deborah and Huldah'.
Sacred History 1.24: Deborah restored Israel after Jabin's 20 years; her deliverance 'a type of the Church'.

saint.text: OCA: 'Righteous Deborah' (entry says only that her story is in Judges 4:5-14 and chapter 5). The OCA lists her on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers (between 11 and 17 December): found on its all-lives pages for 15 December 2024, 14 December 2025 and 13 December 2026, absent from 17 December 2024 and 2025. Her 'December 17' URL is the 1989 Forefathers Sunday. No fixed date, so the page has no feast panel.

No Deborah (or Debbora) in the Roman Martyrology 1916, the 1969 Calendarium, the USCCB 2026 calendar, the Church of England calendar, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 (the Episcopal Church), or the LSB (Missouri Synod).
saint.source: grep of the shared calendar files

saint.text: ELCA, Evangelical Lutheran Worship (2006), prayer 'The saints' names 'Deborah and Gideon' among God's servants and witnesses of times past. Copyrighted: paraphrased on the page, not quoted.

Gallery, wide screens only.

could_not_verify: Whether the current (2004) Roman Martyrology names Deborah: no public copy was fetched. The page says only that the 1916 edition and the calendar used at Mass have no day for her.
A Greek synaxarion day for Deborah: none found; the page names only the OCA's Sunday.
The date of Solimena's painting: not given on Commons; the caption gives none.
Handel's oratorio Deborah (1733) would make a tidbit, but no source was fetched, so it is left out.
left_out: The modern debate over women leading in the church, where Deborah is a central text. Not taken up: it needs each side in its own words, and is the owner's call.
A death section: Judges tells nothing of her end. Josephus's line (she and Barak died about the same time) is a fact; Pseudo-Philo's lament is in What others said, marked as later.
A miracles section: the storm and the stars fighting are told in Her song (Judges 5:4, 20-21, and Josephus), not as wonders she worked.
The Talmud's charge (Pesachim 66b) that she lost her prophecy for boasting 'a mother in Israel': a later rabbinic reading that reads as a slight; not used.
Salomon de Bray's Jael, Deborah and Barak (1635): Jael, with the hammer and a low neckline, fills the picture and Deborah is small behind her.
The Russian icon roundel of Righteous Deborah (Solntsev's chromolithograph): about 180 px, too small.

checker_2026_09_25.checked: One light pass. Read the page whole. Checked: the Catholic Encyclopedia ('deliverers and leaders', the prophecy 'refers not to Debbora herself, but to Jahel'); the Jewish Encyclopedia (the palm tree, Lappidoth as Barak); Britannica ('perhaps the oldest section of the Bible'); the OCA's whole entry for Righteous Deborah; the ELCA prayer for the saints ('Deborah and Gideon'); the 1916 Martyrology, the USCCB, Church of England, Episcopal and LSB calendars (no day); the Talmud's seven prophetesses (Megillah 14a); 1 Samuel 12:11 in the BSB (it does read Barak); Judges 5:2-3 (the song opens at 5:2). Licences: all four Commons files match the page. The hub card is centred with the eyes at about 39%.
changed: The two read titles carried *...* marks, but the template prints a read's title as plain text, so the asterisks would have shown. Removed. (Abigail, Gideon and Ruth have the same in a read title, and Martha and Mary Magdalene in a read's 'by': not this checker's files, reported.)
The Talmud tidbit cited the Jewish Encyclopedia 'Deborah', whose text does not hold the list of seven. It now cites Megillah 14a at Sefaria, where the list is (the evidence entry is updated).

The palm tree tidbit said the rabbis had her judge outdoors 'so that anyone could come'. The Jewish Encyclopedia gives the reason as propriety: being a woman, she would not judge in private. The line now says that.
Myth 2: 'No book of the Bible names Deborah outside Judges 4 and 5' clashed with the page's own 'Other Deborahs' fact. It now says 'No other book of the Bible names her.'
Judges 5:3 was called 'the opening of her song'; the song opens at 5:2. Now 'Near the start of her song'.
